newsitem.title: USA: Rover tangles with rock in first Mars fender-bender.
newsitem.headline: Rover tangles with rock in first Mars fender-bender.

text.p: The Mars rover tangled with a rock four times its size on Thursday in the first Martian fender-bender.

The microwave-size buggy sustained no damage, "and as far as we know Jack Morrison's (driver's) license is still valid," Mission Manager Richard Cook quipped in a reference to the Earth-bound controller of the rover Sojourner.

The rover hit the rock, named "Yogi" by space scientists, as it was backing up and manoeuvring itself to position its alpha proton X-ray spectrometer against a flat surface. It was moving too fast and its left rear wheel rode up on the rock. Its onboard computers, sensing the collision, immediately brought it to a stop, Cook said.
He likened it to a driver backing up to and over a curb.
"This was not unexpected. We saw this in tests on Earth," Cook said.

Justin Maki, a science manager on the Pathfinder team, showed journalists a "movie" made up of several still frames showing the collision. "It (the rover) drove too far. It was a little too enthusiastic," he said.
But the incident delayed the survey of "Yogi," the second in a series of rocks targeted by engineers for analysis by Sojourner.

The analysis, intended to determine the chemical composition of "Yogi," was initially scheduled to take place on Tuesday after the rover had successfully performed a similar inspection of another rock, "Barnacle Bill," and found it resembled rocks on Earth, something scientists had not expected.

Tuesday's analysis was postponed when it was determined from photographs taken by the Mars Pathfinder lander that the front of the rock had an overhang, making any analysis there perilous to the rover.
Scientists pored over the high-resolution pictures for a day before deciding to send the buggy to the left side of the rock, where Wednesday's bump occurred.
Cook said the rover would be instructed to drive forward, away from the rock for a few inches (centimeters) and then reposition itself before starting its analysis on Thursday night.
Scientists are particularly interested in "Yogi" because from the photographs it appears to be of a different composition than that of "Barnacle Bill."
The next target, Cook said at a news briefing at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory, was a white-coloured rock called "Scooby Doo," after the U.S. cartoon character.
Carol Stoker, a participating scientists, said, "We have never before seen a whitish-coloured rock on Mars. It is definitely an important target."
Scientists also want to send Sojourner to a rock called "Deep Red."
The nominal time given for the rover to operate, following last Friday's pin-point landing on Mars, was just a week, but Cook said he expected it to be roving the planet's surface for several weeks.

"That's why we can afford to spend three or four days on one particular rock," he said. The lander and its equipment were expected to be operating and sending signals and pictures back to Earth for several months, scientists said.

Meanwhile scientists continued to analyse the wealth of data from the spaceship. One surprising finding, Mars meteorologist Julio Magalhaes told reporters, was that the upper Martian atmosphere appeared to have cooled somewhat in the last 21 years since the Mars Viking missions.

Measurements taken by the Viking landers and the Pathfinder lander showed that "In the 120-kilometre (75-mile) to 60-kilometre (32-mile) range (above the surface) the atmospheric temperatures got a bit cooler," Magalhaes said.
In particular, Pathfinder recorded temperatures of minus 275 degrees Farenheit (-170 C) at a height of 30 miles (48 km), the coldest ever recorded in the Martian atmosphere.
Meanwhile, the high temperature on the surface on Wednesday was a balmy 8 F (-13 C), plunging to a chilly overnight low of -103 F (-75 C).
